etymology: Hebrew kesil, “fool” or, as a star-name, “Orion,” a town in the Negeb of Judah named among the uttermost cities toward the border of Edom.
biblical_def: Chesil was a town in the south country of Judah, the Negeb, named in the long roll of cities given to the children of Judah by lot when Joshua and Eleazar the priest divided the land. It stands among the uttermost cities of the tribe toward the coast of Edom southward (Jos 15:30), in a dry and thirsty region where the inheritance was measured out to the people of God. The same town appears to be reckoned with Bethul and Hormah among the cities of Simeon, for Simeon’s portion was taken from the midst of the lot of Judah, the part of Judah being too much for them. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little southland town among the goodly heritage He apportioned to His people. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Chesil stands as a witness that no portion of the saint’s heritage, however dry or unremembered, is too small for the care of Him who apportioned it by lot.

etymology: Hebrew madmenah, “dunghill” or “dung-heap,” a town near Jerusalem named in Isaiah’s account of the Assyrian advance; compare Madmannah of the south of Judah.
biblical_def: Madmenah was a town lying on the road by which the Assyrian invader pressed toward Jerusalem, named by the prophet Isaiah in his vivid march of the destroyer through the villages north of the city. The prophet cries that Madmenah is removed, and the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee (Isa 10:31), painting the terror of the people as the rod of Assyria came nearer and nearer to the holy mount. It is to be distinguished from Madmannah, a city of the south country of Judah in the allotment of the tribe (Jos 15:31), though the names are near akin in sound and root. The dictionary does not labour to settle the exact site; what it honours is that even the little towns trembling before the Assyrian were not outside the hand of the LORD, who used the rod of His anger for a season and then broke it. The same God who set the bounds of the people also numbers the hairs of their head, and the flight of Madmenah’s people was seen and ordered by Him. The remnant of Jacob was not delivered by their own walls but by the LORD of hosts, who said that the Assyrian should not come into this city. Madmenah stands as a witness that the providence of God governs the smallest town in the day of trouble.

etymology: Hebrew sekakah, “enclosure” or “thicket,” a town in the wilderness district of Judah named among the six cities with their villages.
biblical_def: Secacah was a town in the wilderness of Judah, named among the six cities set in the desert tract of the tribe’s inheritance when Joshua divided the land by lot. It is listed with Middin, Nibshan, the city of Salt, and En-gedi, six cities with their villages, in that dry and broken country falling away toward the Salt Sea (Jos 15:61-62). This was no green and watered portion, but a wilderness of rock and ravine where few cities could stand; yet even there the LORD planted the dwellings of His people and numbered them in the goodly heritage. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD reckoned even this wilderness town among the inheritance He apportioned to Judah. The lines were fallen unto them in pleasant places, though the place to the eye was a desert, and the bounds of their habitation were the work of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Secacah stands as a witness that the providence of God reaches even into the wilderness, and that no portion of the saint’s heritage, however barren it appear, is forsaken of Him who measured it out.

etymology: Hebrew tsenan, perhaps “place of flocks” or “pointed,” a town in the low country, the Shephelah, of the tribe of Judah.
biblical_def: Zenan was a town in the valley, the Shephelah or low country, of the tribe of Judah, named in the long roll of cities given to the children of Judah by lot when Joshua divided the land. It is listed with Hadashah and Migdal-gad among the cities of the lowland that lay between the hill country of Judah and the plain of the sea (Jos 15:37). This was a fruitful and well-watered region, a contrast to the barren Negeb and wilderness, and many cities with their villages were set there for the people of God. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its situation; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little lowland town among the goodly heritage He apportioned to Judah. Zenan stands as a witness that the providence of God is as careful over the small towns of the fertile valley as over the great cities of the kings, and that no portion of the saint’s heritage, however lightly remembered, falls outside His apportioning hand.

etymology: Hebrew tsephath, “watch-tower” or “look-out,” a Canaanite city of the south that was utterly destroyed and afterward called Hormah.
biblical_def: Zephath was a Canaanite city in the south country, taken and utterly destroyed by the men of Judah and Simeon in the days after the death of Joshua, when the tribes went up to drive out the inhabitants of the land. The children of Judah went with Simeon their brother and slew the Canaanites that inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it; and the name of the city was called Hormah (Jdg 1:17), which is to say, “devoted to destruction.” The new name preserved the memory of the holy war, in which the city was given over to the ban and laid under the curse, a sober witness to the judgment of God upon a people whose iniquity was full. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its site; what it honours is that the conquest of the land was no mere act of human conquest, but the execution of a long-forewarned justice by the hand of His people. The same God who set the bounds of the people also appointed the times of the nations, and when the cup of Canaan was full He removed them and planted Israel in their stead (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Zephath, become Hormah, stands as a witness that the LORD is righteous in His judgments and faithful to His covenant promise.

etymology: Hebrew ’ashan, “smoke,” a town first reckoned to Judah and then to Simeon, afterward given to the Levites of the sons of Aaron.
biblical_def: Ashan was a town of the south country first named in the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, and afterward reckoned among the cities given to the tribe of Simeon, whose portion was taken out of the midst of the lot of Judah, for the part of Judah was too much for them (Jos 15:42; 19:7). In the days of the settled kingdom it was numbered among the cities of refuge and dwelling given to the Levites, to the sons of Aaron the priest, that the tribe which had no land-inheritance might yet have cities to dwell in and suburbs for their cattle (1Ch 6:59). Thus Ashan, whose name signifies smoke, became a place where the priests of the LORD dwelt among the people of Simeon and Judah, a little Levitical town set for the service of the sanctuary. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its site; what it honours is the wisdom of the LORD in scattering the priesthood through the tribes, that every region might have the means of grace and the ministers of the altar near at hand. The same God who set the bounds of the people appointed also that the tribe of Levi should have no inheritance but Himself (Deu 32:8). Ashan stands as a witness that the LORD provides for those who serve Him, and sets His ministry in the midst of His people.

etymology: Hebrew ’ether, perhaps “abundance” or “plenty,” a town of the south reckoned both to Judah and to Simeon.
biblical_def: Ether was a town of the south country, named first in the low cities of the tribe of Judah and afterward reckoned among the cities of the tribe of Simeon, whose inheritance lay within the lot of Judah (Jos 15:42; 19:7). It is listed with Ashan, Remmon, and Ain, four cities and their villages, in the portion measured out to Simeon when his too-great brother Judah yielded part of his ample lot. The name, signifying perhaps abundance or plenty, stood over a small and seldom-named town, as if to remind the reader that the LORD’s abundance is not measured by the greatness of a place in the eyes of men. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its site; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little southland town among the goodly heritage He apportioned to His people. The lines were fallen unto them in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Ether stands as a witness that the abundance of God is poured even into the smallest portion, and that no part of the saint’s heritage is forgotten of Him who apportioned it by lot.

corruption_paragraphs: Ether is a town of the sacred geography, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name among the cities of Simeon within Judah may know it for a real place in a real inheritance, given by a real God to a real people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the abundance of God poured even into the least portion. He who set Ether by lot among the cities of Simeon is the same who has determined the times before appointed and the bounds of every nation and every soul. The saint who feels his portion small may remember Ether, whose very name speaks plenty, and learn that the LORD’s abundance is not measured by the greatness of a place in the eyes of men.

etymology: Hebrew kesulloth, “the loins” or “flanks,” perhaps of a hill, a border town in the allotment of the tribe of Issachar.
biblical_def: Chesulloth was a town in the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar, named in the roll of cities that fell to that tribe by lot when Joshua divided the land among the children of Israel. It is listed with Jezreel and Shunem near the beginning of Issachar’s portion, on the borders toward the valley of Jezreel (Jos 19:18). Issachar’s lot lay in the fruitful plain between the hill of Tabor and the river Jordan, a goodly land of which the patriarch had said that Issachar saw the rest was good, and the land that it was pleasant. The name Chesulloth, signifying the loins or flanks of a hill, may mark its situation upon the lower slopes that gird the great plain. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its site; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little border town among the goodly heritage He apportioned to His people. The lines were fallen unto Issachar in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were the work of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Chesulloth stands as a witness that no portion of the saint’s heritage, however small or unremembered, is overlooked by Him who apportioned it by lot.
